cards.title: Read short-term spikes as gambling products
cards.summary: Distinguish 'gamble' products that blow up just recently from products with sustained revenue history.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a product whose revenue graph shows a recent sharp spike, before committing to test it.
steps: Switch the dashboard to the 180-day view rather than judging from a 7- or 30-day window.
Look for sustained performance, e.g. a product running at ~$2K days since early in the year while also trending up recently: that is much healthier than one that only jumped in the last few days.

If a product was doing lows of a few hundred dollars per day and is essentially spiking now, treat it as a 'gamble product'. The source still tests these sometimes, but frames them as gambles, not validated winners.
Check whether the spike coincides with one very recent piece of content or an older piece that suddenly resurfaced; the latter is a weaker signal.
caveats: A gamble product is a judgment call, not a rule; the presenter explicitly says the risk is his own preference.
Recent spikes can be real demand or a single lucky video; the dashboard alone cannot tell which.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Lower revenue filters to cut competitive products
cards.summary: Narrowing the revenue band to roughly $36K-$70K surfaces less saturated products than a $70K+ band.
cards.use_when: The product list is full of products you've seen advertised many times, or you want less competitive candidates.
steps: Start with a wider revenue range, then notice when results are dominated by products you recognize from being advertised everywhere.
Reduce the band to about $36,000 low and $70,000 high to see far fewer competitors.
Treat the lower band as a healthier hunting ground, but accept smaller upside: a validated product in a less crowded band may scale less than a big branded one.
Verify current dashboard filter behavior before relying on exact thresholds; interfaces change.
caveats: The exact numbers are this presenter's live example, not a universal benchmark.
Low-revenue products can be low-revenue because demand is genuinely small, not only because competition is low.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Screen out non-English creatives before testing
cards.summary: Products whose winning content is in Spanish are a hard skip because they don't transfer to English-speaking audiences.
cards.use_when: Checking a product's top-performing videos during research.
steps: Open the product's last-7-days videos and identify the language of the top creative.
If the best-performing video is in Spanish, disqualify the product for an English-language test — the source has found these do not replicate for English speakers.
Apply the same screen to Spanish-language ads found later in the feed even when the revenue graph looks good.
Also check that live selling has not overtaken the revenue; if a large share comes from live streams rather than regular ads, the ad data is less usable.
caveats: This is the presenter's tested heuristic for English-speaking markets; it says nothing about success when targeting Spanish-speaking audiences.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Check how concentrated the winning videos are
cards.summary: Revenue spread across several videos is healthier than one dominant winning video.
cards.use_when: Judging whether a candidate product's recent sales are repeatable across creative.
steps: Review the individual videos driving the past 7 days of revenue.
Look for distribution like $2K, $1.8K, $1.4K across three different videos: this indicates multiple creatives are working, which is a strong sign.
If a single winning video carries most of the revenue, treat it as more fragile — one video can be luck or an outlier.
Then check the winning video's post date: a video posted a couple of weeks ago that is still scaling is a mild red flag; content posted this week and already performing well is the stronger signal.
caveats: One dominant video can still be a real winner; even revenue spread does not guarantee performance when you test your own offer.
Post dates only tell you about the observed creative, not about the product's long-term demand.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Competitor-set your niche, not just your product
cards.summary: When you sell a variant format you still compete with every other format of the same ingredient or niche.
cards.use_when: Assessing saturation for supplement-style or format-substitution products.
steps: Identify the underlying ingredient or niche (e.g. GLP), not just the exact product (e.g. patches).
Recognize that even if nobody else sells the patch version, you are competing for the same customers who know the powder, gummies, resin, or pills.
Add competitor checks against the niches you compete in as a whole, in addition to the specific product keywords.
Use this to decide whether a healthy-looking graph is actually in a crowded customer pool.
caveats: A niche-wide competitor set will always look large; the point is to price your differentiation, not to avoid the category entirely.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Pressure-test the offer before you sell the same product
cards.summary: Competitor offers often bundle a commodity product into a branded kit; copyable offer structure matters as much as the product.
cards.use_when: You found a product with an appealing graph but generic positioning, and need a differentiation angle.
steps: Click into a competitor's store from the Facebook Ad Library result and inspect the offer page.
Note the structure rather than the product: e.g. a 'youth reset kit' on top of NAD patches, buy-one-get-one-free, plus a free ebook and an eye mask. The presenter rates this structure as strong.

Look for ingredient-level specificity over adjectives: 'youthful' is a vague adjective, while naming an active ingredient (e.g. bee venom, known to the target female audience) tells the customer why the product works.
Use that specificity — plus your own offer stack — as the reason your variant of the same product could still win.
caveats: Strong offers still face the niche-wide competition described elsewhere.
Verify current ad library navigation before assuming a given layout.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Skip products with low perceived-value pricing
cards.summary: Under-$10 price points force matching price and usually fail the perceived-value test.
cards.use_when: A researched product shows a good graph but sells cheaply.
steps: Check the store's selling price, e.g. a bug-bite suction device at $9.99.
If the price is low like that, recognize you will be forced to run the same low-price play, which caps margins and ad economics.
Prefer products with higher perceived value that can support a healthy price band, like the skin-tag removal cream the presenter flagged as well-priced.
Treat low price as a structural constraint on the funnel, not just a number to edit on a test.
caveats: Low-price products can work in volume models; this is the presenter's preference for his drop-shipping tests, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Use the shape of the 180-day graph as a fast filter
cards.summary: Up-down-up with an overall uptrend is healthy; a graph already in the gutter or on a downtrend is not worth testing.
cards.use_when: Scanning many products and deciding which ones deserve a closer look.
steps: Open the 180-day view first and read the overall trend rather than the last blip.

Screen out graphs that are clearly declining — the presenter rejected a tinted lip serum doing $40K in 30 days because the 180-day graph was 'in the gutter', and rejected several others as downtrends.
Keep the products whose graph oscillates but trends up overall.
Only then spend time on videos, competitor lookup and trend checks for the survivors.
caveats: Graph reading is a screening step, not proof of demand transfer to your own store.
Tools, ranges and labels change; confirm what the chart shows in your tool's current version.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Research candidates against Facebook Ad Library and Google Trends
cards.summary: A product counts as validated when it survives both a competitor search and a trend check.
cards.use_when: You have a candidate with a good graph and need a go/no-go before testing.
steps: Search the product keyword in the Facebook Ad Library to gauge how many advertisers are running it right now.
Look for signals like a competitor who launched an ad only hours ago — that shows the space is live and being contested.
Search the product on Google Trends to see whether search interest is building rather than decaying.
Test only if the product looks validated across both checks; if no competition is findable at all, judge whether the trend and recency justify a speculative test.
caveats: Keyword selection is the hard part: for unfamiliar products like gut-cleansing protocols or fulvic acid blends, the obvious terms may surface nothing even when competitors exist.
Absence of visible competitors is ambiguous, not automatically good.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Switch filter categories to find cross-listed winners
cards.summary: A product can appear under a different dashboard category than the niche it truly belongs to, so loosen category filters.
cards.use_when: You are searching a niche and the category filter may be hiding relevant products.
steps: Don't treat the dashboard category as truth: an arnica removal cream can sit under beauty and personal care while functionally being a supplement-driven health product.
When a promising product is not showing in your main category, widen or change the category filter so it can appear.
Once found, evaluate it on the same criteria as everything else: 7-day revenue (~$8K in the example), distribution across videos, price band and untapped feel.
Confirm the product actually has a mechanism story (e.g. removing skin tags) rather than being a random listing.
caveats: Category filters are tool-specific and can change; verify how the platform you use organizes categories today.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Choose niches by competition level, not popularity
cards.summary: Beauty and personal care equals health in potential but also in competition; less-hyped niches like home, tools and appliances often have lower competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding which niche to hunt in before opening the product dashboard.
steps: Treat beauty and personal care as equally viable to the health niche, with the same caveat of being equally competitive.
Also consider women's wear and underwear, men's wear and underwear, home supplies, tools and hardware, home improvement and household appliances — niches the presenter says have low competition.
Recognize that not hearing about a niche is the point: few sellers are in it, so a product with real revenue behind it is close to a validated winner.
Expect fewer candidates per session in these niches because the option pool is smaller, and sift routinely rather than expecting every product to be good.
caveats: The presenter also notes these niches can attract passionate buyers and more product options, but quality still varies product by product.
Low competition is not the same as proven demand; the revenue graph still has to be there.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Beware recognizable products and brands
cards.summary: If you've seen the product or brand many times — in ads or as an established retailer — pass on it.
cards.use_when: A candidate looks familiar or comes from a long-established brand.
steps: During scanning, treat your own familiarity as a red flag: the presenter skipped a known natural shampoo brand because it has been around a long time and isn't worth testing.
Do the same for products you've personally seen advertised before (e.g. a deworming protocol ad the presenter recalled), since many other advertisers are likely running them too.

Confirm with the competitor check: a shilajit-and-collagen bundle graph looked healthy, but the presenter rejected it because he knows the product and expects heavy competition in Facebook Ad Library.
Keep scanning rather than trying to out-execute a saturated, well-known product.
caveats: Familiarity is a heuristic for saturation, not proof; a familiar category can still contain an untapped variant.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Decide whether to keep hunting or switch niches
cards.summary: If pages of results are duds, adjust filters or switch niche rather than quitting early.
cards.use_when: You have scrolled several result pages without a candidate worth testing.
steps: Check how deep you actually are: the presenter refused to give up at page five of a many-page list.
If duds dominate while your filters look reasonable, widen or change the category filter rather than assuming the whole niche is dead.
Only switch niche after adjusting filters and still finding nothing — the presenter did this after the health niche run.
Remember speed compounds: as you repeat this, you will no longer need a walkthrough video, and a single session can plausibly surface two or three strong candidates.
caveats: There is no fixed number of pages that means 'give up'; the source only warns against quitting too early.
Sessions can produce zero winners, and that is a normal research outcome, not a failure of the method.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Accept that validated products can still fail your test
cards.summary: Testing a validated product on Meta with your own ads and offer is a new experiment, not a guaranteed win.
cards.use_when: Planning a product test after research signals look strong.
steps: Recognize the gap: the product was validated on its own store with its own content, while you test on Meta with more edited ads and a different offer.
Treat research as generating candidates worth a test, not as evidence of certain success.
If the test fails, reuse the same research method to find the next candidate rather than abandoning the process.
Run the test for about 2-3 days on Meta, then assess and move on to the next product if it did badly.
caveats: The 2-3 day assessment window is the presenter's own practice for drop-shipping tests, not a universal statistical standard.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx
